images.title: Prime or composite?
images.purpose: Show that a prime has only two factors, so its dots make just one row, while a composite number can also make a rectangle.
images.composition: Two panels side by side with a wide gap: a single row of dots on the left, a small rectangle of dots on the right, each with a short caption.
exact_structure: Left panel: exactly 7 teal (#0072B2) dots in one straight row; caption 7 = 1 × 7 below; the word prime in green (#009E73) below that.
Right panel: exactly 6 amber (#E69F00) dots arranged in 2 rows of 3; caption 6 = 2 × 3 below; the word composite in vermilion (#D55E00) below that.
No other dots, no grid lines, no other numbers.
rejection: any number of dots other than 7 on the left or 6 on the right
the 7 dots arranged in more than one row
the 6 dots arranged other than 2 rows of 3
images.takeaway: A prime has only 1 and itself as factors, while a composite number has more.
images.description: Seven teal dots in a single row labelled prime beside six amber dots in 2 rows of 3 labelled composite.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Ask whether 7 dots can be put in a rectangle with more than one row; then discuss why 1 is neither prime nor composite.

image_decisions.why: A dot array gives a visual test for prime versus composite that students can reuse.
